items.stem: Water molecules are polar because:
choices: The oxygen atom attracts the shared electrons more strongly than the hydrogens
The hydrogen atoms attract electrons more strongly
The molecule has no net charge
items.note: Unequal sharing in the O–H covalent bonds gives oxygen a partial negative charge and the hydrogens partial positive — the basis of hydrogen bonding and every water property.

items.stem: Cohesion between water molecules is caused by:
choices: Hydrogen bonds between the polar molecules
The oxygen atoms bonding to each other
items.note: Hydrogen bonds between the partially positive H and partially negative O of neighbouring molecules. Consequences: surface tension and water transport under tension in xylem.

items.stem: The solvent properties of water are important for life because:
choices: Water dissolves the lipids in membranes
Most metabolic reactions occur in aqueous solution — polar molecules dissolve readily
Non-polar molecules dissolve best in water
items.note: Water's polarity makes it an effective solvent for polar/hydrophilic molecules. Hydrophobic molecules (lipids) are insoluble — which is also exploited (membranes).

items.stem: Ice floats on liquid water because:
choices: Hydrogen bonds hold the molecules in an open lattice that is less dense than liquid water
Solutes in ice make it lighter
items.note: As water freezes, hydrogen bonds lock molecules into a lattice with more space between them → lower density. This insulates water below, allowing aquatic life to survive under ice.

items.stem: Water's high specific heat capacity benefits aquatic organisms because:
choices: Water heats and cools very quickly
Temperature changes slowly, providing stable habitats
items.note: Much energy is needed to raise water's temperature — aquatic environments are thermally stable. Also high latent heat of vaporization: evaporative cooling.

items.stem: Which property of water allows insects to walk on the surface of ponds?
items.note: Cohesion at the water–air surface creates surface tension — dense enough to support light organisms (water striders).

items.stem: The monomer unit of polysaccharides such as starch, glycogen and cellulose is:
items.note: All three are polymers of glucose — but with different linkages (alpha vs beta) and branching, which determines whether they are storage or structural.

items.stem: Which disaccharide is formed from glucose and fructose?
items.note: Sucrose = glucose + fructose (table sugar, transported in plants). Maltose = glucose + glucose; lactose = glucose + galactose.

items.stem: Glycogen differs from amylose (starch) because glycogen is:
choices: More highly branched, allowing rapid glucose release
A structural molecule in plant cell walls
items.note: Glycogen (animals/fungi) is highly branched → many ends for fast enzyme access → quick glucose mobilization. Starch is the plant storage polysaccharide.

items.stem: Cellulose is suitable as a structural material in plant cell walls because:
choices: Its straight chains of beta-glucose form hydrogen-bonded bundles with high tensile strength
It is highly branched and soluble
items.note: Cellulose: straight (beta-glucose, every second molecule inverted), cross-linked by hydrogen bonds into microfibrils → strong walls. Contrast with helical alpha-glucose starch.

items.stem: Lipids store approximately twice as much energy per gram as carbohydrates because:
choices: Lipids are richer in carbon–hydrogen bonds and less oxidized
items.note: Fatty acid hydrocarbon chains are energy-rich. Also: lipids provide insulation and buoyancy (whale blubber) and are stored without water (1 g glycogen stores water with it).

items.stem: A triglyceride is formed by condensation reactions between:
choices: Glycerol and three fatty acids, producing ester bonds
Two amino acids, producing a peptide bond
items.note: Glycerol's three –OH groups + three fatty acid –COOH groups → three ester bonds + 3 water. Condensation always releases water.

items.stem: Unsaturated fatty acids tend to be liquid at room temperature because:
choices: They are shorter than saturated fats
Cis double bonds kink the hydrocarbon chain, preventing tight packing
items.note: Cis double bonds create kinks → weaker packing → lower melting point (oils). Trans fats pack like saturated fats — linked to health risks.

items.stem: Phospholipids differ from triglycerides because one fatty acid is replaced by:
items.note: The polar phosphate head + non-polar tails make phospholipids amphipathic → bilayers. The single most important molecule for membrane structure.

items.stem: The general structure of an amino acid includes a central carbon bonded to:
choices: An amine group, a carboxyl group, hydrogen and an R group
Two carboxyl groups and an R group
A phosphate, a sugar and a base
items.note: The R group is what differs between the 20 amino acids — it determines the protein's properties (polar, non-polar, charged).

items.stem: The bond linking two amino acids in a dipeptide is formed by:
choices: Condensation between the amine of one and the carboxyl of the other, releasing water
Sharing of electrons between R groups
Ionic bonding of the two carboxyl groups
items.note: Peptide bond: condensation reaction between the amine group and the carboxyl group, releasing water. Breaking it back requires hydrolysis.

items.stem: Denaturation of a protein involves:
choices: Permanent disruption of the tertiary structure, losing function
items.note: Heat/pH break the weak bonds holding the 3D shape — the sequence (primary structure, peptide bonds) stays intact but the shape and function are lost.

items.stem: A nucleotide consists of:
choices: A phosphate group, a pentose sugar and a nitrogenous base
An amine group and a carboxyl group
items.note: Three components: phosphate, pentose sugar (deoxyribose in DNA, ribose in RNA), nitrogenous base (A, T/U, C, G).

items.stem: In DNA, adenine always pairs with thymine using:
items.note: A–T: two hydrogen bonds. G–C: three — which is why DNA regions rich in G–C are harder to separate.

items.stem: RNA differs from DNA because RNA:
choices: Contains ribose and uracil instead of deoxyribose and thymine
Has phosphate groups in the middle of the strand
items.note: Three differences: sugar (ribose), base (uracil replaces thymine), structure (single-stranded, usually). mRNA, tRNA and rRNA are the main types.

items.stem: Compare the structure and function of starch, glycogen and cellulose in plants and animals.
markscheme: All three are polysaccharides of glucose — same monomer, different bonding (1)
Starch: alpha-glucose; storage in plants, in plastids/chloroplasts (1)
Glycogen: alpha-glucose, more highly branched than starch; storage in animals, in liver and muscle (1)
Branching = many free ends → rapid glucose mobilization for both storage polysaccharides (1)
Cellulose: straight chains of beta-glucose, cross-linked by hydrogen bonds into microfibrils → structural function in cell walls (1)
Humans can digest starch (alpha linkages) but not cellulose (beta linkages — lack of cellulase) (1)
items.tactic: Compare questions need BOTH sides for every point: same monomer, different linkage → different shape → different function. Structure–function links earn the marks.

items.stem: Explain three properties of water that make it essential for life, referring to its molecular structure.
markscheme: Polarity + hydrogen bonding → excellent solvent for polar molecules → metabolic reactions in solution (1)
Cohesion due to hydrogen bonds → water transport under tension in xylem and surface tension habitats (1)
High specific heat capacity — hydrogen bonds absorb energy → stable temperatures for enzymes and aquatic habitats (1)
High latent heat of vaporization → evaporative cooling (sweating, transpiration) (1)
Ice less dense → floats, insulating water below (1)
items.tactic: Property → cause (hydrogen bonding/polarity) → biological consequence. Name the property, then the living-world example.

items.stem: Which property of water allows it to be pulled up the xylem in one unbroken column?
choices: Cohesion — hydrogen bonds between water molecules
items.note: Cohesion holds the water column together under tension; adhesion to the walls supports it. Both act together in the transpiration stream.

items.stem: In a hydrolysis reaction, water acts as:
choices: A reactant that splits the polymer
items.note: Hydrolysis = breaking with water: one water molecule is consumed per bond split. Condensation is the reverse (releases water).

items.stem: Adhesion of water to xylem walls helps by:
choices: Supporting the water column against gravity
items.note: Adhesion (water–wall hydrogen bonds) counters gravity's pull on the column, especially in narrow vessels.

items.stem: Evaporative cooling by sweating works because water has a:
choices: High latent heat of vaporization — much energy is absorbed as water evaporates
items.note: Each evaporating water molecule takes substantial energy from the skin surface — effective cooling without denaturing enzymes (moderate loss only).

items.stem: Glucose, fructose and galactose all have the formula C₆H₁₂O₆ — they are therefore:
items.note: Same molecular formula, different structural arrangement → different properties. Isomerism recurs throughout organic chemistry.

items.stem: Trans-fatty acids are considered harmful mainly because:
choices: The trans double bond straightens the chain, making them behave like saturated fats in membranes
items.note: Trans configuration = hydrogens on opposite sides of the C=C → straighter chain → packs like saturated fats → raises LDL cholesterol.

items.stem: Which protein is primarily STRUCTURAL?
items.note: Collagen: triple helix, tensile strength in skin/tendons/bones — structural. Hemoglobin transports, insulin is hormonal, amylase catalyses.

items.stem: Adenine and guanine are classified as:
items.note: Purines: A and G (fused double ring, larger). Pyrimidines: C, T and U (single ring). Purine always pairs with a pyrimidine — constant strand width.
